citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a Banach space. It has the **approximation property** (AP) if for
every norm-compact set $C\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a
bounded finite-rank operator $T:X\to X$ such that

$$\sup_{x\in C}\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon.$$

Here finite rank means that $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional.

For $\lambda\ge0$, $X$ has the **$\lambda$-bounded approximation property**
($\lambda$-BAP) if the same assertion holds with the additional operator-norm
bound $\|T\|\le\lambda$, where the norm is that of [[def-operator-norm]]. It
has the **bounded approximation property** (BAP) if it has $\lambda$-BAP for
some finite $\lambda$.

No sequence of approximating operators is required; this matters in
nonseparable spaces. Plainly $\lambda$-BAP implies AP.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K \in \{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and the complex case by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. Let
$e:n\to X$ be an ordered basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and write $e_j:=e(j)$.
Give $\mathbb K^n$ its coordinate $\ell^1$ norm

$$\|(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})\|_1:=\sum_{j<n}|a_j|.$$

Define

$$T:\mathbb K^n\to X,\qquad T(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})=\sum_{j<n} a_j e_j.$$

Then $T$ is a topological isomorphism of normed spaces in the sense of
[[def-topological-isomorphism-of-normed-spaces]].

derivations.claim: If $K$ is empty use zero maps. Otherwise consider all pairs $(x,\rho)$ with $x\in K$ and $\rho>0$ such that $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/4$ whenever $\|z-x\|_X<3\rho$. Continuity ensures that the balls $B(x,\rho)$ from this family cover $K$; take a finite subcover $B(x_i,\rho_i)$. Put $\delta=\min_i\rho_i>0$. For $x\in K$ and $z\in X$ with $\|z-x\|_X<\delta$, select $i$ with $\|x-x_i\|_X<\rho_i$; then both $x,z$ lie within $3\rho_i$ of $x_i$, so $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. No compact neighborhood of $K$ is asserted or needed.

Apply AP in $X$ to choose bounded finite-rank $P$ with $\sup_K\|Px-x\|_X<\delta$. By step 1.1, $\sup_K\|T(Px)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. The set $T(P(K))$ is compact; apply AP in $Y$ to obtain bounded finite-rank $Q$ with $\sup_{x\in K}\|QT(Px)-T(Px)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. Thus $QT P$ approximates $T$ on $K$ within $\varepsilon$. This makes only two AP selections and does not require a sequence, an infinite union of compact sets, or a choice principle for sequences.

Choose a finite basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_J$ of $P(X)$. Its coordinate functionals are bounded by [F2]; hence $Px=\sum_j\ell_j(x)\alpha_j$ with $\ell_j$ bounded on $X$, by composing those functionals with $P$. Write $Rz=\sum_jz_j\alpha_j$, $E(x)=(\ell_j(x))_j$. Choose a finite basis $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_s$ of $Q(Y)$, with bounded coordinate functionals $c_i$, and put $h_i(z)=c_i(QT(Rz))$ and $Bv=\sum_i v_i\beta_i$. Each $h_i$ is continuous on all $\mathbb R^J$, and $BhE=QTP$. For a zero-dimensional range use one zero basis vector and the zero coefficient map instead of an actual basis. These formulas prove the stated factorization and complete the proof.

citations.quote:
1.1 If $D=\varnothing$, $X$ is the zero space and $F=0$ has all the required properties; if $K=\varnothing$, $F=0$ suffices as well. Henceforth both sets are nonempty. In particular $0<|D|<\infty$, because $D$ contains a ball and is bounded. Fix one boundary chart $Q$, with Lipschitz graph function $\varphi$ of constant $L$, and an ambient neighborhood $U$ of its boundary point with $\bar U\subset Q$ compact. In chart coordinates set $v=(L+2)e_d$. For $x\in\bar D\cap\bar U$, $|z|\le1$, and sufficiently small $t>0$, uniformly in $x,z$, the point $y=x+tv-tz$ stays in $Q$ because $t(|v|+1)<\operatorname{dist}(\bar U,Q^c)$. Moreover $y_d-\varphi(y')\ge x_d-\varphi(x')+t(L+2)-t|z_d|-Lt|z'|\ge t>0$. Thus $\overline B(x+tv,t)\Subset D$. Rotate $v$ back to the original coordinates. [given, F7, F8, construct, algebra]

1.2 The compact boundary admits finitely many such $U_j$, $1\le j\le J$, covering it. The compact remainder $\bar D\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^JU_j$ lies in $D$; cover it by finitely many balls with closures in $D$, and let $U_0$ be their union, omitting it if the remainder is empty. Then $\bar U_0\Subset D$, so $v_0=0$ has the same ball property for sufficiently small $t$. Apply [F2] to this finite open cover of $\bar D$, obtaining $\psi_j\in C_c^\infty(U_j)$ with $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$. The minimum of the finitely many positive bounds on $t$ gives $t_0>0$ such that $\overline B(x+tv_j,t)\Subset D$ for every $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$ and $0<t<t_0$. Taking the family of all admissible chart neighborhoods before extracting a finite subcover avoids selecting a chart independently at every boundary point. [F2, F7, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 By [F9] choose a nonnegative smooth bump compactly supported in $B_1(0)$ and positive on $\overline B_{1/2}(0)$, and divide it by its positive integral to obtain $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0))$ with $\int\rho=1$. Put $\rho_t(w)=t^{-d}\rho(w/t)$. Every $u\in X$ belongs continuously to $L^1(D)$: use [F8] for Sobolev spaces, and $\|u\|_1\le |D|\|u\|_{C^m}$ for $C^m$. For its zero extension $E_0u$ define $H_{j,t}u(x)=(\rho_t*E_0u)(x+tv_j)$ and $S_tu=\sum_j\psi_jH_{j,t}u$. By [F4] these are well-defined linear constructions independent of representatives and $S_tu\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. [F4, F8, F9, step 1.2, construct]

2.2 First take $X=W^{m,p}(D)$. For every $|\gamma|\le m$ and $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, [F3] and step 1.2 give
$$D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)=\int\rho(z)(E_0D^\gamma u)(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz.$$
The translated center has distance greater than $t$ from $D^c$: the entire closed ball of radius $t$ is a compact subset of $D$. The identity consequently holds on a neighborhood of each indicated $x$. Equivalently the defining weak-derivative identity can be tested against $y\mapsto\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, whose support is compact in $D$; its two derivative signs cancel. Only interior values are used, with no assertion that derivatives commute with zero extension across $\partial D$. [F1, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1]

2.3 For $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ define $T_{j,t}f(x)=\int\rho(z)f(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz$ and $\omega_f(r)=\sup_{|h|\le r}\|f(\cdot+h)-f\|_p$. Translation invariance and [F5] give $\|T_{j,t}f\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ and
$$\|T_{j,t}f-f\|_p\le\omega_f((|v_j|+1)t).$$
By [F4], $\omega_f(r)\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$. The integral estimates also apply when $p=1$, where [F5] follows directly from Tonelli. [F4, F5, step 2.1, construct]

2.4 Set $f_\gamma=E_0D^\gamma u$. The finite Leibniz rule [F6], step 2.2 and $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$ give, for $|\alpha|\le m$, the a.e. identity on $D$
$$D^\alpha(S_tu-u)=\sum_j\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\psi_j)\bigl(T_{j,t}f_{\alpha-\beta}-D^{\alpha-\beta}u\bigr).$$
Every derivative $D^\beta\psi_j$ vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, so step 2.2 supplies exactly the identities used in this formula. All these fixed multiplier derivatives are bounded. Step 2.3 and the finite norm sum [F1] therefore imply $\|S_tu-u\|_{W^{m,p}}\to0$. The same Leibniz formula without subtracting $u$, and $\|T_{j,t}f_\gamma\|_p\le\|f_\gamma\|_p\le\|u\|_{W^{m,p}}$, give $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$. For example take the $\ell^p$ norm over $\alpha$ of $\sum_{j,\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}\|D^\beta\psi_j\|_\infty$. This argument includes $m=0$ and $p=1$. [F1, F6, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra]

3.1 Now take $X=C^m(\bar D)$. By [F6] each bounded classical derivative is its weak derivative, so $u\in W^{m,1}(D)$ and step 2.2 applies. Each $D^\gamma u$ is uniformly continuous on $\bar D$ by [F7]. For $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, every sampled $y=x+t(v_j-z)$ lies in $D$ and $|y-x|\le(|v_j|+1)t$. Positivity and mass one of $\rho$ thus give
$$\sup_{x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j}|D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)-D^\gamma u(x)|\le\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\bar D\\|x-y|\le(|v_j|+1)t}}|D^\gamma u(y)-D^\gamma u(x)|\longrightarrow0.$$
The formula of step 2.4, first on $D$ and then by continuity on $\bar D$, gives $\|S_tu-u\|_{C^m}\to0$. Bounding each averaged derivative by $\|D^\gamma u\|_\infty$ and summing the same fixed multiplier constants gives $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$ also in this case. [F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 2.4, algebra]

4.1 Fix $0<t<t_0$. Write $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, so $S_tu(x)=\int_D k_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Fix a closed box $Q$ containing $\bar D$. The finitely many $D_x^\alpha k_t$, $|\alpha|\le m$, are smooth and uniformly continuous on the compact set $\bar D\times Q$ by [F7]. For any $\eta>0$, partition $Q$ into finitely many measurable cells $Q_\ell$ of small enough diameter, assigning shared and outer faces consistently, and choose $y_\ell\in Q_\ell$. Their diameters can be chosen so that $|D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y)-D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y_\ell)|<\eta$ for $x\in\bar D$, $y\in Q_\ell$ and $|\alpha|\le m$. The point $y_\ell$ need not lie in $D$. [F7, step 2.1, construct]

4.2 Define
$$F_{t,\eta}u(x)=\sum_\ell k_t(x,y_\ell)\int_{D\cap Q_\ell}u(y)\,dy.$$
Each coefficient is a bounded linear functional by step 2.1, and there are finitely many coefficients. Each range function $k_t(\cdot,y_\ell)$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, so the operator has finite rank with the required smooth range. Comparison with the integral for $S_t$ gives
$$\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha(F_{t,\eta}-S_t)u|\le\eta\|u\|_{L^1(D)}.$$
For $X=C^m(\bar D)$, this yields $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le |D|\eta$. For $X=W^{m,p}(D)$ let $A_m$ be the finite number of multi-indices of order at most $m$. Taking the derivative $L^p$ norms and then applying [F8] gives $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le A_m^{1/p}|D|^{1/p}\eta |D|^{1-1/p}=A_m^{1/p}|D|\eta$. This includes $p=1$, and it shows each $F_{t,\eta}$ is bounded because $S_t$ is bounded. [F1, F8, step 2.1, step 2.4, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 By steps 2.4 and 3.1 the operators $S_t:X\to X$ converge pointwise to the identity and satisfy $\|S_t\|\le M_X$. Choose $\delta<\varepsilon/[4(M_X+1)]$. Compactness gives a finite $\delta$-net $u_1,\ldots,u_N$ in $K$. Pointwise convergence permits one $t\in(0,t_0)$ such that $\max_i\|S_tu_i-u_i\|<\varepsilon/4$. For any $u\in K$, choose one net point within $\delta$; then $\|S_tu-u\|\le(M_X+1)\delta+\max_i\|S_tu_i-u_i\|<\varepsilon/2$. Compactness also makes $R=\sup_{u\in K}\|u\|$ finite: a finite cover by unit balls bounds all these norms by one plus the largest center norm. [step 2.4, step 3.1, given, choose, algebra]

5.2 Choose $\eta>0$ small enough that the relevant bound in step 4.2 is below $\varepsilon/[2(R+1)]$. For $F=F_{t,\eta}$,
$$\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|\le\|F-S_t\|R+\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|<\varepsilon.$$
Its range is a finite span of ambient compactly supported smooth functions by step 4.2. Applying this conclusion to the singleton compact set $K=\{u\}$ proves smooth-restriction density for every $u\in X$. All net, partition and representative-point choices here are finite; Countable Choice enters only the analytical interfaces stated above. [step 4.2, step 5.1, choose, algebra] ∎

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

derivations.claim: Empty $K$ or $L=0$ is handled by $\kappa=0$. Otherwise [F1] permits choosing $t>0$ with $\sup_K\|S_ta-a\|_X<\varepsilon/(2\|L\|)$. For fixed $t$, the map $y\mapsto k_t(\cdot,y)|_D$ is ambient $C^\infty$ with values in $X$: every mixed $x$ and $y$ derivative is uniformly continuous on compact products, so the ordinary finite-dimensional Taylor remainders in $y$, uniformly for $x$ derivatives through order $m$, tend to zero in the $C^m$ norm and hence in the $X$ norm. Thus $\kappa_t(y)=L(k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$ is ambient smooth, with $D_y^\alpha\kappa_t=L(D_y^\alpha k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$. It is bounded on $\bar D$.

For each $a\in X$, one has $L(S_ta)=\int_D\kappa_t(y)a(y)\,dy$. To justify the identity without assuming a vector-integration theorem, partition a box containing $D$ into cells of diameter tending to zero and replace $k_t(\cdot,y)$ on each cell by $k_t(\cdot,y_l)$. Uniform continuity of every $x$ derivative through order $m$ makes the error in $X$ at most $c_X\eta\|a\|_1$, where $\eta\to0$ is the uniform kernel derivative error and $c_X$ converts a $C^m$ bound to an $X$ bound. Applying bounded $L$ to the finite sums is legitimate by linearity. Their scalar integral errors are at most $\|L\|c_X\eta\|a\|_1$ as well, so passing to the limit proves the identity. Consequently $\sup_K|L(a)-\int_D\kappa_ta|<\varepsilon/2$.

Compactness of $K$ in $X$ implies its compactness in $L^1(D)$ by [F2]. Given $\theta>0$, take a finite $\theta/2$ net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ in that $L^1$ image. By integrability and an exhaustion of $D$ by compact subsets, there is one compact $F\subset D$ with $\int_{D\setminus F}|a_i|<\theta/2$ for all $i$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\int_{D\setminus F}|a|<\theta$. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\le\zeta\le1$, compactly supported in $D$, equal to one on $F$; use [F3] for the one-set open cover $\{D\}$ of $F$. Then $\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\theta$. This uses a finite net and finitely many integrable tails, including at $p=1$; it requires no $L^\infty$ approximation of a dual coefficient.

If $\|\kappa_t\|_{L^\infty(D)}=0$, choose $\kappa=0$. Otherwise use step 2.1 with $\theta=\varepsilon/(2\|\kappa_t\|_\infty)$ and set $\kappa=\zeta\kappa_t\in C_c^\infty(D)$. The cutoff error satisfies $\sup_K|\int_D(\kappa_t-\kappa)a|\le\|\kappa_t\|_\infty\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 1.2 proves the claim.

citations.quote:
Fix an input dimension $q\ge1$ and an integer $m\ge0$. Let $\mathcal A_m^{(q)}$ be the class of continuous scalar activations $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ for which there is one depth $n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, the scalar-output depth-$n$ multilayer perceptrons with activation $\sigma$ are dense in $C^m(K)$ in the $C^m$ norm. For vector outputs, stack scalar-output networks of that same depth. The source notation $\mathcal A_m$ suppresses the input dimension fixed by the finite-dimensional network under consideration. Let $\mathcal A_m^{L,(q)}$ be the subclass whose members are Borel measurable and have at most linear growth, meaning
$$\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\frac{|\sigma(s)|}{1+|s|}<\infty.$$
For an integer $q\ge1$, define $\mathrm{BA}_q$ to consist of those $\sigma\in\mathcal A_0^{(q)}$ for which, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, there is a finite multilayer perceptron $f:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with
$$|f(x)-x|_2\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in K),\qquad |f(x)|_2\le C\quad(x\in\mathbb R^q).$$
Here $\operatorname{diam}_2(K)=\sup_{x,y\in K}|x-y|_2$. The diameter-based global bound is part of this definition and is retained verbatim; its nonemptiness is checked separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and Lipschitz, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.
For each $q\ge1$, the class $\mathrm{BA}_q$ in the displayed activation-class definition is empty.

derivations.claim: If $K$ is empty choose the zero operator. Otherwise put $T=G^\dagger|_K$ and choose $0<\tau<\varepsilon/5$. Every listed input space injects continuously into $L^1(D)$: for finite $p$, $\|a\|_1\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|a\|_p\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|a\|_{W^{m,p}}$ when applicable, and for $C(\bar D)$ use $\|a\|_1\le|D|\|a\|_\infty$. Thus each smooth moment $a\mapsto\int_D\varphi a$ is continuous on $A$ and such moments separate distinct members of $K$, using [F4]; distinct continuous functions also differ on an interior set of positive measure.

The set $Q=\{(a,b)\in K^2:\|T(a)-T(b)\|_U\ge\tau\}$ is compact. For each pair in $Q$ a separating moment from step 1.1 remains nonzero on a neighborhood of that pair. A finite subcover supplies moments $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_J$ such that $E(a)=(\int_D\varphi_ja)_{j=1}^J$ has $E(a)\ne E(b)$ for all $(a,b)\in Q$. If $Q$ is nonempty, the positive continuous function $|E(a)-E(b)|_2$ on $Q$ has a positive minimum $r$; if $Q$ is empty set $J=1$, $\varphi_1=0$, and $r=1$. In both cases $|E(a)-E(b)|_2<r$ implies $\|T(a)-T(b)\|_U<\tau$. This is the complete finite-moment reduction and does not presume a dual representation theorem.

Cover the compact $E(K)$ by finitely many open balls of radius $r/4$ with centers $z_i=E(a_i)$, $a_i\in K$, $1\le i\le s$. Put $h_i(z)=\max(0,r/2-|z-z_i|_2)$, $h_0(z)=\operatorname{dist}(z,E(K))$, and $w_i(z)=h_i(z)/(h_0(z)+\sum_{k=1}^s h_k(z))$. The denominator is positive everywhere: off $E(K)$ its first term is positive, and on $E(K)$ some $h_i>r/4$. Consequently $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_s)$ is continuous on all $\mathbb R^J$, nonnegative, and $\sum_iw_i\le1$, with equality on $E(K)$. For $a\in K$, $w_i(E(a))>0$ implies $|E(a)-E(a_i)|_2<r/2$ and hence $\|T(a)-T(a_i)\|_U<\tau$. The convex combination $\sum_iw_i(E(a))T(a_i)$ therefore differs from $T(a)$ by less than $\tau$.

For Lebesgue and Sobolev outputs choose smooth neighborhood restrictions $\phi_i$ with $\|\phi_i-T(a_i)\|_U<\tau$, using [F3]. For continuous outputs set $\phi_i=T(a_i)$, which is already $C^{m_2}(\bar D')$. Define $Bv=\sum_i v_i\phi_i$ and $L=\max(1,\|B\|_{\ell^1\to U})$. Since the weights in step 1.3 sum to one on $E(K)$, $\sup_K\|T(a)-Bw(E(a))\|_U<2\tau$. This is the output finite-dimensional factorization.

Let $Z=\{z:\operatorname{dist}(z,E(K))\le1\}$, a compact subset of $\mathbb R^J$. Uniform continuity of $w$ on $Z$ gives $0<\delta<1$ such that $z,z'\in Z$ and $|z-z'|_2<\delta$ imply $|w(z)-w(z')|_1<\tau/L$. Set $R=\max(1,\sup_{a\in K}\|a\|_1)$. By the $\sigma_2$ premise [F1] choose common-depth scalar networks $p_j$ with $\sup_{\bar D}|p_j-\varphi_j|<\delta/(2R\sqrt J)$. Then $\widetilde E(a)=(\int_Dp_j(y)a(y)\,dy)_j$ satisfies $\sup_K|\widetilde E-E|_2<\delta/2$, so $\widetilde E(K)\subset Z$ and $\sup_K\|Bw(E(a))-Bw(\widetilde E(a))\|_U<\tau$. The input layer kernel $(x,y)\mapsto(p_j(y))_j$ ignores $x$ and has exactly constant spatial output. The estimate uses only $L^1$ bounds and covers $p_1=1$.

Apply the $\sigma_1\in\mathcal A_0$ premise to the continuous map $w$ on compact $\widetilde E(K)$, obtaining a finite MLP $f:\mathbb R^J\to\mathbb R^s$ such that $\sup_{z\in\widetilde E(K)}|f(z)-w(z)|_1<\tau/L$. Then $\sup_K\|Bw(\widetilde E(a))-Bf(\widetilde E(a))\|_U<\tau$. Only $C^0$ approximation of this middle map is used; no differentiability of $\sigma_1$ is needed.

Put $V=\max(1,\sup_{a\in K}|f(\widetilde E(a))|_1)$, finite by continuity and compactness. Define $c_U=1$ for $U=C^{m_2}(\bar D')$ with the maximum derivative norm, and $c_U=(J_{m_2}|D'|)^{1/p_2}$ for $U=W^{m_2,p_2}(D')$ with the usual sum-of-$p_2$-powers norm, where $J_m$ counts multi-indices of order at most $m$; this also treats $L^{p_2}$ with $J_0=1$. For $C^{m_2}$ functions $u$, directly integrating each derivative gives $\|u\|_U\le c_U\|u\|_{C^{m_2}}$. By $\sigma_3\in\mathcal A_{m_2}$ choose common-depth networks $q_i$ such that $\|q_i-\phi_i\|_{C^{m_2}(\bar D')}<\tau/(c_UV)$. These approximants are chosen from the $C^{m_2}$ network subfamily supplied by that density premise, so their derivatives exist. With $\widetilde Bv=\sum_i v_iq_i$, the estimate $\|(\widetilde B-B)v\|_U\le c_U|v|_1\max_i\|q_i-\phi_i\|_{C^{m_2}}$ yields $\sup_K\|\widetilde Bf(\widetilde E(a))-Bf(\widetilde E(a))\|_U<\tau$. Equivalent choices of standard Banach norms merely change $c_U$.

Write the middle MLP as $f(z)=A_{n+1}\sigma_1(A_n\sigma_1(\cdots\sigma_1(A_1z+b_1)\cdots)+b_n)+b_{n+1}$ with $n$ hidden layers. On a spatially constant field $v(y)=z$, the affine map $z\mapsto Az+b$ is represented exactly by the integral kernel $A/|D|$ and constant bias $b$. Such constants are exact $\sigma_2$ networks through their output biases. Use these layers after the input layer of step 2.2, placing precisely the $n$ coordinatewise $\sigma_1$ activations of $f$ between them. The final kernel $\kappa(x,y)=|D|^{-1}(q_1(x),\ldots,q_s(x))$ is a $\sigma_3$ network ignoring $y$, so its integral over $D$ sends a constant $v$ to $\widetilde Bv$. This proves that $G(a)=\widetilde Bf(\widetilde E(a))$ belongs to $\mathrm{NO}_{n+2}$ under the indexing convention in [F2]. All intermediate fields are constant and the final output belongs to $U$ for every $a\in A$.

Adding the four errors in steps 2.1–2.4 gives $\sup_K\|T(a)-G(a)\|_U<5\tau<\varepsilon$. This proves the core theorem. The proof in fact only needs continuity of $T$ on $K$ and the continuous injective $L^1$ realization of $A$; it retains all the listed source spaces.

For the corrected additional branch assume $U$ Hilbert, $M>0$, and $\sup_A\|G^\dagger(a)\|_U\le M$. Apply the core construction with an error $0<\gamma<\min(M,\varepsilon/2)$, calling the resulting operator $G_0$. It has the exact form $G_0(a)=\sum_i f_i(\widetilde E(a))q_i$. Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ for the finite-dimensional span of the $q_i$, discarding linear dependences, and express $G_0(a)=\sum_jg_j(\widetilde E(a))e_j$. Each $g_j$ is a linear combination of the $f_i$ and hence the same-depth $\sigma_1$ MLP; each $e_j$ is a linear combination of the $q_i$ and hence a same-depth $\sigma_3$ network. If the span is zero the zero operator already suffices. Otherwise $|g(\widetilde E(a))|_2=\|G_0(a)\|_U<M+\gamma<2M$ on $K$.

The set $S=g(\widetilde E(K))$ is compact with radius at most $2M$. Apply the explicitly corrected property in the Statement with $C=2M$ and tolerance $0<\eta<\varepsilon-\gamma$, obtaining $b$. Compose its $\sigma_1$ MLP with $g$ and use final kernel $|D|^{-1}(e_j(x))_j$. By step 3.1 this is an operator $G_1$ of the required architecture. Orthonormality gives $\sup_K\|G_1-G_0\|_U<\eta$ and $\|G_1(a)\|_U=|b(g(\widetilde E(a)))|_2\le2M\le4M$ for every $a\in A$. Thus its approximation error is below $\gamma+\eta<\varepsilon$. The argument handles arbitrary positive $M$ without the source's unjustified normalization $M\ge1$.

The corrected property has concrete instances. For ReLU and a compact $S\subset\mathbb R^q$, suppose $C\ge\sup_S|z|_2$. If $S$ is empty choose zero. If $C=0$, then $S\subset\{0\}$ and again choose zero. If $C>0$, the coordinate clamp $c_j(z)=-C+\operatorname{ReLU}(z_j+C)-\operatorname{ReLU}(z_j-C)$ is an exact ReLU network onto $[-C,C]^q$ and fixes $S$. The radial projection $P$ onto the Euclidean ball of radius $C$ is continuous and fixes $S$. By [F6] approximate $P$ on the cube by a ReLU MLP $p$ with Euclidean error $<\xi$, where $0<2\xi<\eta$. Then $b(z)=Cp(c(z))/(C+\xi)$ is a finite ReLU MLP, globally bounded by $C$, and for $z\in S$ its error is less than $\xi+\xi C/(C+\xi)<2\xi<\eta$. Composition of layered MLPs is a layered MLP because consecutive affine maps merge. ReLU also has linear growth and belongs to every relevant $\mathcal A_0$ by [F6]. Thus this corrected branch is nonvacuous.

For the exact printed additional implication the premise $\sigma_1\in\mathrm{BA}$ is impossible by [F5], so that implication is true but has no instances. Steps 4.1–4.2 establish the explicitly different nonvacuous branch; neither step alters the diameter-based class. This completes all asserted implications.
